Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
The assault happened in the late afternoon of a Tuesday in late autumn, inside the small, cluttered office of a man who had been his supervisor for three years. For Marcus, the memory did not fade or blur with time. He could still feel the precise pressure of the hand on his shoulder, the way the man’s other arm had pinned his arm to the desk, the smell of coffee and old paper. He remembered the fluorescent light flickering overhead and the sound of his own breathing, ragged and shallow. But there were gaps, too—black spaces where the sequence of events should have been. He knew what had happened, but when he tried to tell anyone, the words would not come. His mouth would go dry, his throat would close, and he would shake his head, unable to form a sentence that would make sense.

In the months that followed, Marcus began to notice that his body no longer felt like his own. He had come to believe that it had betrayed him, that it had frozen when it should have fought, that it had been weak when it should have been strong. He could not trust it anymore. Every unexpected touch—a colleague’s hand on his arm, a student leaning too close to his desk—sent a jolt through him, sharp and electric, as though the skin itself remembered. He began to avoid physical contact altogether. He stopped shaking hands. He sat at the far end of the tutoring center’s long table, his back to the wall, a chair placed so that no one could approach him from behind. He did not think of this as a choice; it felt like survival.

His work as a tutor required him to be alone with students in quiet rooms, and that had become impossible. He could not sit with a young man in a closed office without his heart racing, without his eyes darting to the door, without his mind cataloging every exit and every object that could serve as a barrier. He started to watch his students closely—not for academic confusion, but for signs of threat. A shift in posture, a hand moving under the table, a voice that dropped too low. He knew this was not rational, but he was certain that danger was everywhere, that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. He began to avoid unfamiliar places entirely. He drove the same route to work every day, ate at the same two restaurants, shopped at the same grocery store. If a friend suggested a new café or a different park, Marcus would say no, and he would not explain why.

The isolation crept in slowly. He stopped returning calls from old friends. He declined invitations to holiday gatherings and weekend dinners. He had come to feel that he existed in a different world from other people, that they could not possibly understand what it meant to live inside a body that could not be trusted, inside a memory that would not let go. He smoked more than he used to, sometimes a pack a day, standing alone on the back porch of his small apartment, watching the neighbors through the fence.

What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon in November, four years after the assault. He was tutoring a new student, a young man in his early twenties, and the student had reached across the table to point at a worksheet. His hand had brushed Marcus’s wrist. Marcus had stood up so fast his chair had fallen over. He had walked out of the room without a word, his hands shaking, his chest tight, and he had not gone back. He spent the rest of the day in his car, parked in a lot behind a strip mall, trying to find the words to describe what had happened and failing. He was afraid that he would never be able to work again, that he would spend the rest of his life watching the space around him for threats that might not be there. He was afraid that the gaps in his memory would never fill in, that he would always be caught between the vivid clarity of that afternoon and the emptiness where the rest of the story should be. He wanted to stop being afraid of his own body. He wanted to sit in a room with another person and not feel like he was about to die.
